title: St Nicholas (6 December)
hookLine: shoes by the door and small gifts for children

cards: A pair of small shoes sits by the front door, left out overnight on purpose. In the morning there's something tucked inside: an orange, a few chocolate coins wrapped in gold foil, maybe a little toy.

Nobody saw who put them there. That's the point. In parts of Europe, children set out their shoes, or hang a stocking, on the eve of St Nicholas's day, and wake up to find that someone came in the night.
The custom is sweet and small, and it hides a serious old story about money, shame, and a window left open in the dark.

teach.b: Nicholas was a bishop of Myra, a town on the southern coast of what is now Turkey. Much of what people tell about him comes from tradition, and it's honest to say so. The best-known story goes like this.
A father in his town has lost everything. He has daughters, and no money for their dowries, so no one will marry them, and the family faces ruin and disgrace. Nicholas hears about it.
He doesn't knock or make a speech.

teach.h: GOLD THROUGH THE WINDOW AT NIGHT.
teach.b: At night he tosses a bag of gold through the window, and slips away. The story says he came back again, so the father hid, watched, and finally caught him. And Nicholas asked him to tell no one.

teach.h: LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.
teach.b: The story acts out a saying of Jesus from the Sermon on the Mount: "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly."
Giving in secret protects the one who receives. The father doesn't have to thank a rich man in the street. And it protects the giver too, from the small pleasure of being seen being good.
Orthodox, Catholic and some other churches keep Nicholas's day as a feast.
Even people who keep no saints' days may know a version of him, because some trace the Christmas gift-bringer called Santa Claus back to this bishop.
Underneath the red suit is a man throwing money through a window and running away.

how: In some countries children put out shoes or stockings on the eve of St Nicholas's day and find small gifts in the morning; Orthodox and Catholic churches keep his feast with prayers and hymns.

s: the story of the gold through the window comes from tradition, not the Bible
the Bible never mentions Nicholas; the story is how tradition remembers him.
in the story, Nicholas handed the gold over in public so the town could see
he threw it through the window at night and asked not to be named.
the saying about the left and right hand comes from the Sermon on the Mount
Matthew 6:3: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth."

games.q: you're Nicholas. a father in your town can't pay his daughters' dowries and his family faces disgrace. you have gold. what do you do?
o: give it to him in front of the town, so others learn to give.
lend it to him and ask for it back later.
throw it through his window at night and tell no one.
games.why: tradition says he tossed the gold through the window in the dark, and when the father caught him, asked him to keep it secret.

practice: Let someone come to mind who has had a hard week, a neighbor, a coworker, a person at the bus stop, and imagine a small gift no one could trace back to you: a paid-for coffee, a note with no name, coins where a child will find them.
If you pray, you can hold that person before God for a moment; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: St Nicholas. A bishop of Myra, remembered for gifts given at night through a window, and for asking that nobody be told.

carryVoice: Your line: give in secret. The left hand never needs to know. Until tomorrow.
